HJM Term Structure Model — Project Report

A plain-language walkthrough of the model and what its currently calibrated parameters actually are, generated 2026-09-04 15:12 EDT directly from this repository's data.

Abstract

This report presents a Heath-Jarrow-Morton (HJM) model of the US Treasury yield curve: a computer model of the entire curve — not just the handful of maturities the government actually reports, but every point in between — evolving realistically through time under a no-arbitrage constraint. The curve's dimensionality is reduced in two stages: a Nelson-Siegel fit compresses each day's 11-tenor curve (from 0.0833-year to 30-year) down to 3 shape parameters, which are then rotated via Principal Component Analysis (PCA) into 3 statistically independent factors, ranked by how much of the curve's combined movement each one explains. Each factor is modeled as a mean-reverting (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck) process and calibrated on 6,546 daily observations spanning 2001-07-31 to 2026-09-01, then used to simulate no-arbitrage forward paths for the full curve. Where noted, forecast accuracy is validated by a walk-forward backtest against a held-out region of that history, benchmarked against a naive random-walk forecast and a standard machine-learning baseline, with results reported by horizon rather than collapsed into one headline figure. Every figure and number in this report is generated from the project's own currently calibrated state, not illustrative examples.

Introduction

US Treasury yields are observed at only a handful of maturities — a 1-month bill, a 2-year note, a 10-year bond, and so on — yet most practical work with interest rates (pricing, hedging, stress testing) needs the entire curve, at every maturity, evolving realistically through time. A curve model has to satisfy three requirements at once: it must fit the maturities actually observed, stay smooth in between them, and evolve over time without creating arbitrage — a situation where two parts of the curve are priced inconsistently enough that a riskless profit could be locked in just by trading between them. Simple interpolation methods satisfy the first two requirements but say nothing about the third: they describe a shape, not a process that stays internally consistent as time passes and rates move.

The Heath-Jarrow-Morton (HJM) framework resolves this by modeling the whole forward curve as a single evolving stochastic process, instead of picking a curve shape and re-fitting it snapshot by snapshot. Its key result: once the curve's volatility structure is specified — how much, and in what correlated way, different maturities move — the drift each maturity must follow is no longer a free choice. It is pinned down directly by the no-arbitrage condition, rather than imposed as a separate rule. What remains is a practical difficulty, not a theoretical one: the forward curve has infinitely many maturities, so specifying an independent volatility for each is infeasible — there isn't enough data, and naive attempts overfit noise into an unstable model. The rest of this report addresses that difficulty directly: reducing the curve to a small number of interpretable factors, calibrating their dynamics against real data, and validating the result against what the curve actually did next.

The raw data: yield curves over time

Each line below is one day's observed Treasury yield curve — the interest rate the government pays, at that moment, for every maturity from a few months out to 30 years. The shape moves around: it flattens, steepens, and occasionally inverts (short-term rates above long-term ones) as the economy and monetary policy change. A single number, like "the 10-year rate," misses almost all of this — which is the whole reason for building a model of the curve rather than tracking one point on it.

The five snapshots below are hand-picked, not evenly sampled, to show that range of shapes: the legend labels each one with its curve shape — steep, flat, or inverted — computed directly from that day's actual 10-year/2-year spread (the standard "2s10s" market shorthand).

Finding the patterns: Principal Component Analysis

Almost all of the curve's day-to-day movement turns out to follow a handful of repeating patterns — commonly described as the whole curve shifting up or down (level), tilting between short and long maturities (slope), and bending in the middle (curvature). Principal Component Analysis (PCA) finds these patterns statistically, ranked by how much of the curve's actual historical movement each one explains.

FactorVariance explainedCumulative
PC149.7%49.7%
PC228.1%77.8%
PC322.2%100.0%

All 3 factors together necessarily explain 100.0% of the variation in those 3 curve-shape numbers — PCA isn't discarding anything here, just rotating them into statistically independent, ranked-by-importance directions. The real dimensionality reduction already happened upstream, fitting 3 numbers to the whole observed curve instead of tracking every tenor independently.

How the factors behave: mean reversion

Each factor doesn't wander off forever — historically, when one drifts away from its long-run average, it tends to drift back. That behavior is modeled as an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process, fit separately to each factor's history. Three numbers describe it: how fast it reverts (kappa), what it reverts to (theta), and how much it jitters along the way (sigma) — summarized here as a half-life: roughly how many trading days it takes a displacement to shrink by half.

FactorkappathetasigmaHalf-life (days)
PC10.42 0.0081.104 417
PC21.25 0.0041.454 140
PC30.30 -0.0000.629 584

These are point estimates — the single best-fit number for each parameter, from a standard method (maximum likelihood) that reports no sense of how uncertain that number actually is. The next section addresses that directly.

How sure are we? Bayesian parameter uncertainty

The point estimates above are a best guess from a finite, noisy sample — not a known truth. Instead of fitting one number per parameter, this section fits a distribution of plausible values via MCMC (Markov Chain Monte Carlo, using PyMC), then summarizes it as a posterior mean and a 90% credible interval: the range that plausibly contains the true value given the data and the model's assumptions.

Factorkappa (mean)90% interval Half-life (days)r̂ (convergence)
PC10.41 [0.16, 0.66] 421 1.010
PC21.17 [0.65, 1.65] 149 1.000
PC30.31 [0.07, 0.52] 565 1.010

The r̂ column is a convergence diagnostic — it should sit close to 1.00 for the fit to be trusted; a value far from 1 would mean the MCMC chains never agreed with each other and the numbers above shouldn't be relied on. Note how much wider some of these intervals are than the single point estimate suggests: that width is real information the point estimate alone was hiding. The project's README documents, on the full simulation, how propagating this uncertainty through to simulated future rates widens the predictive range by roughly 5-10%.

Connecting factors back to real rates

A move in one of the abstract factors above has to translate into an actual change in forward interest rates at every maturity. This figure shows exactly that translation: how much a one-unit move in each factor shifts the forward rate at each point on the curve. A factor that loads heavily on short maturities but not long ones, for instance, mostly reflects near-term rate expectations rather than a broad shift in the whole curve.

Putting it together: simulating the future

With the factors' dynamics calibrated, the model can simulate many possible future paths for the whole yield curve — 200 of them here, one year ahead, starting from the most recently observed curve. This isn't a prediction of what rates will do; it's the range of curve shapes that are consistent with how the factors have historically behaved, which is what makes it useful for scenario generation and stress testing rather than point forecasting.

How accurate is this, really?

Everything above describes the pipeline's mechanics and shows what it produces. This section is the only part of the report that checks whether any of it actually works: a walk-forward backtest that refits the whole pipeline at each of a series of past dates using only data available up to that date, simulates forward, and compares the result to what the curve actually did next. Restricted here to this project's held-out test region (2024 onward -- see registry/backtest_spec.py), the only span whose results this project treats as a reportable number rather than something used to help design the model.

Two baselines, so "the model's RMSE is 0.004" means something: a naive random walk (tomorrow's curve equals today's), and a RandomForestRegressor fit fresh at every origin on lagged rate levels -- a standard tabular ML point forecaster, walk-forward disciplined the same way everything else here is.

Horizon (days)OriginsRMSENaive RMSE Skill vs. naiveML RMSESkill vs. ML Coverage [95% CI]
21320.0022 0.0019-17% 0.0031+29% 100% [99%, 100%]
63300.0034 0.0035+2% 0.0043+22% 100% [99%, 100%]
126270.0041 0.0045+8% 0.0069+41% 100% [99%, 100%]
252210.0042 0.0059+30% 0.0072+42% 100% [98%, 100%]

Three different questions, three different answers -- "skill vs. X" is the fraction of RMSE the model removes relative to baseline X; the table above pools across tenors, and the per-tenor breakdown (scripts/run_backtest.py --multi-horizon) fills in the rest.

  • The model's uncertainty quantification: coverage is significantly above the nominal 90% at every horizon tested (the 95% CI never dips below 98%) -- the simulated band looks wider than it needs to be to hit 90%, not just luckily calibrated -- see the per-horizon confidence interval in the table, not just the point estimate, since a few dozen origins per horizon is a small enough sample that it matters.
  • Its point forecast against a naive random walk (tomorrow's curve equals today's): skill vs. naive is positive at the 63, 126, 252-day horizons but negative at the 21-day horizon. Interest rates are famously hard to beat with a point forecast -- close enough to a random walk that a negative reading at some horizons isn't obviously a sign of a broken model.
  • Its point forecast against a standard ML baseline: skill vs. ML, pooled across tenors, is positive at every horizon tested. That a parametric, theory-informed model holds its own against a generic tabular learner trained the same walk-forward way is informative regardless of which one edges out the naive baseline -- but pooling across tenors can hide a mixed per-tenor picture, so treat this as a headline, not the full result (see scripts/run_backtest.py --multi-horizon for the per-tenor breakdown).

Reported as found rather than collapsed into one headline number: coverage, skill vs. naive, and skill vs. ML are three different questions with three different answers above, and a model's calibration, its edge over "assume nothing changes," and its edge over a generic ML baseline don't have to agree with each other -- picking just one of the three to report would overstate or understate what this model can actually do. The confidence interval on coverage also treats each origin as independent, which consecutive overlapping-window origins aren't quite -- see TODO.md.

What this model doesn't do

In the interest of not overstating what's here:

  • This simulation runs under the real-world ("P") measure by default — it describes plausible future curve shapes, not risk-neutral prices a trader could hedge against. A risk-neutral ("Q" measure) mode exists, but the market price of risk it would need is deliberately left at zero rather than calibrated — this project only has spot Treasury yields, not the derivative prices that would be needed to estimate it honestly (see TODO.md).
  • The Bayesian section above fits each factor's uncertainty independently, then (when propagated into simulation) pairs draws across factors somewhat arbitrarily — it is not a sample from a true joint posterior over all factors at once.
  • This is a research and educational model, not a production pricing system — see the README's Scope section.

How the code is put together

Everything above is the model explained from the outside — what it does and what it produces. This closing section explains it from the inside: how the ~30 modules behind those results are organized, the sequence they run in, and where deliberate engineering choices, not just modeling ones, are doing work.

Package tour

Nine packages under project/, each with one job:

PackageRoleKey files
registry/Single source of truth for every tunable constant: FRED series codes, the maturity grid, Nelson-Siegel optimizer bounds, PCA factor count, and the backtest's train/validation/test split dates. Nothing else hardcodes these -- every consumer takes them as a default, not a hard constraint, so tests can still pass in tiny synthetic values.paths.py, curve_spec.py, factor_spec.py, market_data.py, backtest_spec.py
data_processing/Fetches raw Treasury yields from FRED and turns them into a clean daily panel: percentage-to-decimal conversion, forward-fill of short gaps, and a data-quality diagnostic (stale runs, outlier jumps via a robust median-absolute-deviation z-score).loaders.py, cleaning.py, io.py
curves/The Nelson-Siegel curve math: one canonical forward-rate/yield formula, two ways to fit it per day (a global optimizer, or -- with the decay parameter held fixed -- an exact linear regression), and a QuantLib benchmark comparing the fitted shape against an independent reference implementation.nelson_siegel.py, quantlib_benchmark.py
transform/Pure, stateless conversions between the three ways a curve gets represented here -- PCA scores, Nelson-Siegel parameters, and forward/zero curves -- shared by both calibration and simulation so each conversion exists exactly once.representations.py
calibration/Turns the daily NS-parameter panel into a compact statistical model: PCA factor extraction, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck mean-reversion fitting both as a point estimate and as a full MCMC posterior, the PC-to-forward-rate sensitivity chain rule, and calibration-quality diagnostics like out-of-sample PCA reconstruction error.pca.py, ou_process.py, bayesian_ou.py, sensitivities.py, diagnostics.py
stochastic/The model itself: HJMModel/HJMModelParams and the Monte Carlo simulation (plug-in and parameter-uncertainty-aware versions), a same-sample plausibility check, and the walk-forward, out-of-sample backtest behind the accuracy section above -- which also fits a naive random-walk and a RandomForestRegressor baseline at every origin, so the model's numbers have something to be compared against.hjm_model.py, validation.py, backtest.py
persistence/Thin save/load functions for every calibrated artifact under data/ns_parameters/. No computation happens here -- it exists purely so calibration code and file I/O stay separate.artifacts.py
viz/One file per domain (curves, PCA, OU, sensitivities, simulation, backtest), each returning a figure object rather than displaying or saving it -- the caller decides what happens to it.curves.py, pca.py, ou.py, sensitivities.py, simulation.py, backtest.py, style.py
reporting/This report generator -- pulls together every other package's output into the document you're reading.report_builder.py

Outside project/: scripts/ holds three runnable entry points (refresh the raw data, generate this report, run the backtest from the command line); notebooks/ holds one narrative notebook that ties every package above together in execution order, each cell just a few lines calling already-tested project/ functions rather than containing logic of its own; tests/ holds 73 tests (one, hitting the live FRED API, skipped by default; several more marked slow for real MCMC or multi-origin backtest runs, which still run by default); and .github/workflows/ holds a scheduled CI job that re-fetches Treasury data and fails loudly on a data-quality flag.

The pipeline, in code

The sequence every one of this report's numbers ultimately comes from:

  1. data_processing.loaders.fetch_treasury_yields pulls raw yields from FRED; cleaning.clean_treasury_yields converts to decimal and forward-fills short gaps.
  2. curves.nelson_siegel.calibrate_all_days_fixed_lambda fits every day's curve to 3 Nelson-Siegel shape parameters via exact linear regression, lambda held fixed across the panel.
  3. calibration.pca.fit_pca rotates that 3-column panel into statistically independent factors.
  4. calibration.ou_process.estimate_ou_parameters_for_factors (point estimate) and/or calibration.bayesian_ou.fit_bayesian_ou_for_factors (full posterior via PyMC) fit each factor's mean-reversion.
  5. calibration.sensitivities.compute_forward_sensitivities chain-rules PCA loadings through the NS formula to get forward-rate sensitivity per factor.
  6. persistence.artifacts.save_* writes every artifact above to data/ns_parameters/; HJMModel.from_disk() reads them back into an in-memory HJMModelParams.
  7. HJMModel.simulate() (or simulate_with_parameter_uncertainty()) evolves the factors forward under the chosen measure and reconstructs a full curve at every step.
  8. stochastic.backtest.run_backtest repeats steps 2-7 at each of a series of historical origins, using only data available up to that origin, alongside a naive random-walk forecast and a fresh RandomForestRegressor baseline (_fit_ml_baseline_at_origin) fit the same way, then scores all three against what actually happened next -- the source of the accuracy section above.

Where this follows good engineering practice

  • Separation of concerns enforced by directory structure, not just convention: pure computation (calibration/, curves/, stochastic/, transform/) never touches disk or draws a plot -- that's persistence/'s and viz/'s job respectively.
  • Typed, structured state instead of loose dicts: HJMModelParams, PCAFactorModel, and SimulationResult are all dataclasses with named fields, not positional tuples or bare dictionaries passed between functions.
  • Pure, dependency-injected constructors: HJMModel takes an in-memory HJMModelParams rather than reading files itself, specifically so it's unit-testable with tiny synthetic parameters -- HJMModel.from_disk() is a convenience classmethod layered on top, not the only way in.
  • Layered, honest testing: fast synthetic-fixture unit tests are the default; a small number of tests marked slow run real MCMC sampling or a real multi-origin backtest and check statistical properties (e.g. credible-interval coverage across replications) rather than trusting a single lucky seed; a dedicated regression test exists specifically to catch a backtest accidentally leaking future data into a past forecast.
  • Mistakes are documented, not hidden: TODO.md and several module docstrings record approaches that were tried and rejected (a day-to-day curve-smoothing penalty), and bugs that were found and fixed after they'd already produced a wrong number -- including the simulator's missing initial-state bug that this report's own backtest section exists partly to have caught.
  • Tooling: pre-commit runs Black and basic hygiene checks (trailing whitespace, end-of-file, a large-file guard) on every commit; DVC tracks the raw data file so it can change without bloating git history; a scheduled GitHub Actions job keeps the data fresh and flags quality problems automatically.
  • Baseline choices are specific, not "add some ML": the backtest's random forest was picked over gradient boosting explicitly because it needs fewer hyperparameters tuned well to be a fair baseline with only a few hundred training rows and no separate validation split -- see _fit_ml_baseline_at_origin's docstring for the full reasoning.
  • Labels stay honest by construction, not by discipline: the "Steep/Flat/Inverted" word in the yield-curve figure's legend is computed from each snapshot's actual 10-year/2-year spread at render time (viz.curves._classify_curve_shape), not hand-typed -- so a future data refresh can't silently leave a stale shape label attached to a curve that no longer has that shape.
